lines: Here's a trap worth knowing before you ever touch a line of code.
A total can pass every sanity check you'd think to run, and still be wrong, because the mistake isn't in the arithmetic at all.
It's in a question nobody asked: has every machine that fed this total actually stayed where the report assumes it was?
A plant's systems split into five levels, and the split has nothing to do with org charts.
At the bottom sits the physical process itself, and above it the devices that sense and touch it directly.
Above that, the controllers that supervise in real time, then the systems that manage a shift's worth of operations, then business planning at the top.
What actually separates these levels is how fast each one has to react, from a fraction of a second at the bottom to weeks at the top.
Here's a real disagreement worth sitting with, not smoothing over.
The standard's own page places supervisory control and data acquisition at the manufacturing-operations level, right next to the systems that schedule production.
Plenty of practitioner diagrams draw that exact same system one level lower, next to the controllers it actually talks to.
Both can't be the one official placement, so what's left standing once you set the disagreement aside?
What's left is the idea neither side disputes: a level is a time horizon, not a specific box, and that's the part worth keeping.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
Imagine the record of every machine's location is flawless: never late, never out of date, right down to the second.
Someone now asks a question not about this second, but about months ago.
Does a flawless record of the present have any business answering a question about the past?
answer: It doesn't, and that holds even with a table that's never a moment out of date.
A table that only remembers where a machine is right now has no way to answer where it was earlier.
Unless the lookup itself carries that earlier time into the join, the current row is simply the wrong row to ask.

lines: Here's how that time actually gets carried.
One physical press ends up with two separate rows in the hierarchy table.
One row for its time on the first line, one for its time on the second, each with its own window of validity and its own generated key.
The move itself isn't an edit to the old row at all. It's a brand new row, sitting right alongside it.
Time to settle it with an actual run, not just an argument.
Take one honest join that respects the reading's own moment, and one careless join that doesn't bother asking when anything happened.
Point both of them at the identical pile of readings, nothing else changed.
What comes out the other side is two different answers for the same two lines, and the gap between them is the entire cost of skipping that one question.
So what was actually doing the work in that correct join?
The machine's own identifier is identical no matter which of its two hierarchy rows you look at.
What tells the join which row answers for which reading is the generated key paired with that row's own window of validity.
The identity by itself was never going to be enough to carry that information.
Five levels split by how fast each one has to react, not by which department owns it.
A real disagreement about where supervisory control sits, settled by the one idea both sides share.
A hierarchy that writes itself a new row every time a machine moves, rather than editing the old one in place.
And a measured join bug that silently moves real output from one line to another without touching a single reading.
A new dashboard caches each machine's current line once a day, and joins every incoming reading against that cache, however old the reading is.
Is a reading from a few days back, from before today's refresh, guaranteed to land on the right line?
answer: It isn't, and the cache being only a day old doesn't rescue it.
The cache answers where a machine is right now, which is exactly the wrong question for a reading from before the move it just learned about.
That cache needs the same thing the join needed from the very start: the reading's own timestamp, carried into the lookup.
